title: x-Smooth Numbers
content: A natural number $n$ is $x$-smooth (also called $x$-friable) if all its prime factors satisfy $p \leq x$. Equivalently, $n$ factors completely over the primes up to $x$. The Dickman function $\rho(u)$ governs the density of $x$-smooth numbers up to $N$ when $x = N^{1/u}$: the proportion is approximately $\rho(u)$ for large $N$. For example, 1-smooth is just $\{1\}$, 2-smooth numbers are powers of 2, and 3-smooth numbers (also called regular numbers) are of the form $2^a \cdot 3^b$.
mathContext: $\text{IsSmooth}(n, x) \iff \forall p \text{ prime},\; p \mid n \implies p \leq x$. The count $\Psi(N, x) = |\{n \leq N : n \text{ is } x\text{-smooth}\}| \sim N \cdot \rho(\log N / \log x)$.

title: Smooth Block of Consecutive Integers
content: A block $n+1, n+2, \ldots, n+k$ is $x$-smooth if every element in the block is $x$-smooth. Finding blocks of consecutive smooth numbers is related to the distribution of primes: if no prime in $(x, n+k]$ divides any element of the block, all elements factor over primes $\leq x$. The existence of such blocks for positive density of $n$ is controlled by the smoothness threshold $S(k)$.

title: Smooth Block Set
content: The set $\{n : \text{SmoothBlock}(n, k, x)\}$ collects all starting points $n$ where the next $k$ consecutive integers are all $x$-smooth. The size of this set (measured by upper density) determines whether $x$ is large enough for the threshold $S(k)$.
mathContext: $\text{smoothBlockSet}(k, x) = \{n \in \mathbb{N} : n+1, \ldots, n+k \text{ are all } x\text{-smooth}\}$

title: Upper Density
content: The upper density $\overline{d}(S) = \limsup_{N \to \infty} |S \cap [N]| / N$ measures the asymptotic 'thickness' of a set $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. A set has positive upper density if $\overline{d}(S) > 0$, meaning it contains a definite fraction of all integers. This is weaker than having positive natural density (which requires the limit to exist). The formalization uses Lean's `Filter.limsup` on the `atTop` filter.

title: Smoothness Threshold S(k)
content: The function $S(k)$ is defined as the minimal $x$ such that the smooth block set $\{n : n+1, \ldots, n+k \text{ are } x\text{-smooth}\}$ has positive upper density. This is the central object of Problem #929. The definition uses `Nat.find` on the existential witness $x = k+1$ (the trivial upper bound). The threshold captures the fundamental tension: making $x$ larger includes more smooth numbers but the goal is to determine the minimal $x$ that suffices.

title: Erdős's Conjecture: S(k) ≥ k^{1-o(1)}
content: The main open question: Is $S(k) \geq k^{1-\varepsilon}$ for every $\varepsilon > 0$ and all sufficiently large $k$? This would mean the smoothness threshold is nearly linear—to guarantee a positive density of $n$ with $k$ consecutive smooth numbers, you need a smoothness bound nearly as large as $k$ itself. This is formalized as an axiom since the problem is OPEN. The $\varepsilon$-$N$ formulation captures the little-$o$ condition: $\log S(k) / \log k \to 1$.
mathContext: $\forall \varepsilon > 0,\; \exists K,\; \forall k \geq K:\; S(k) \geq k^{1-\varepsilon}$, equivalently $S(k) \geq k^{1-o(1)}$

title: Trivial Upper Bound: S(k) ≤ k+1
content: Take $n \equiv -1 \pmod{(k+1)!}$, so $n + i \equiv i - 1 \pmod{i!}$ for $1 \leq i \leq k$. In particular, $i \mid (n+i)$ for each $i$, and all prime factors of $n+i$ that exceed $k+1$ can be handled since the Chinese Remainder Theorem ensures enough such $n$ exist with positive density. Actually, the simpler argument: for $n = m \cdot (k+1)! - 1$, we have $i \mid (n+i)$ since $i \mid i \cdot m \cdot (k+1)!/i$, so each $n+i$ has all prime factors $\leq k+1$.
mathContext: $S(k) \leq k + 1$. Proof: $n \equiv -1 \pmod{(k+1)!} \implies \forall i \in [k],\; i \mid (n+i)$, so each $n+i$ is $(k+1)$-smooth.

title: Rosser's Sieve Lower Bound
content: Rosser's sieve (a refinement of the Brun sieve) shows $S(k) > k^{1/2 - \varepsilon}$ for any $\varepsilon > 0$ and large $k$. The idea: if $x < k^{1/2 - \varepsilon}$, then the primes in $(x, k]$ are too numerous for every element $n+1, \ldots, n+k$ to avoid them all. Sieve methods bound the proportion of integers divisible only by small primes, and when $x$ is too small relative to $k$, the sieve shows no block of length $k$ can be entirely $x$-smooth with positive density. This gives the best known unconditional lower bound.
mathContext: $S(k) \geq k^{1/2 - \varepsilon}$ for all $\varepsilon > 0$ and $k \gg_\varepsilon 1$. Equivalently $S(k) > k^{1/2 - o(1)}$.

title: Ford-Green-Konyagin-Maynard-Tao Upper Bound
content: The groundbreaking 2018 result of Ford, Green, Konyagin, Maynard, and Tao on large gaps between primes implies $S(k) \ll k \cdot \log_3 k / (\log_2 k \cdot \log_4 k)$ where $\log_j$ denotes the $j$-fold iterated logarithm. Their work showed that prime gaps as large as $c \cdot \log p \cdot \log_2 p \cdot \log_4 p / \log_3 p$ occur infinitely often, which translates to bounds on how many consecutive integers can simultaneously be smooth. This is the best known upper bound, improving the trivial $S(k) \leq k+1$ by iterated logarithmic factors.
mathContext: $S(k) \leq C \cdot k \cdot \frac{\log\log\log k}{\log\log k \cdot \log\log\log\log k}$ for some absolute $C > 0$ and large $k$.

title: Monotonicity of S(k)
content: If $k_1 \leq k_2$ then $S(k_1) \leq S(k_2)$: requiring more consecutive smooth numbers (a longer block) can only increase the smoothness threshold needed. This follows because $\text{SmoothBlock}(n, k_2, x) \implies \text{SmoothBlock}(n, k_1, x)$ (a smooth block of length $k_2$ contains a smooth block of length $k_1$), so the density condition is harder to satisfy for larger $k$.

title: Base Case: S(2) = 3
content: The smallest non-trivial case: $S(2) = 3$, meaning 3 is the minimal $x$ such that a positive density of $n$ have both $n+1$ and $n+2$ being $x$-smooth. For $x = 3$, we need both $n+1$ and $n+2$ to be 3-smooth (of the form $2^a \cdot 3^b$). The pairs of consecutive 3-smooth numbers $(2^a 3^b, 2^c 3^d)$ with $|2^a 3^b - 2^c 3^d| = 1$ include (1,2), (2,3), (3,4), (8,9), (80,81), ... (related to Størmer's theorem on consecutive smooth numbers). For $x = 2$, we would need consecutive powers of 2, but the only such pair is (1,2), giving density 0.
mathContext: $S(2) = 3$. The set $\{n : n+1, n+2 \text{ both } 3\text{-smooth}\}$ has positive upper density, but $\{n : n+1, n+2 \text{ both } 2\text{-smooth}\}$ has density 0.
